title: Masculine, feminine, and adjectives that change too
goal: Understand that every Urdu noun has a gender, and that adjectives ending in ـا change to match it — while other adjectives never change at all.
bekal: guess a noun's gender from its ending
name jobs in both masculine and feminine forms

dialogs.title: مکالمہ — یونیورسٹی کے کیفے میں
dialogs.intro: The campus café in Lahore, midday. Every table is full, and someone is standing next to an empty chair.

lines.text: معاف کیجیے، کیا یہ کرسی خالی ہے؟
lines.baca: ma'āf kījiye, kyā ye kursī ḵālī hai?
lines.id: Excuse me, is this chair free?
lines.literal: pardon do-please, Q this chair empty is?

lines.speaker: عائشہ:
lines.text: شکریہ۔ میرا نام عائشہ ہے۔ میں طالبہ ہوں۔

lines.baca: āp kī urdū bahut achchhī hai!

lines.text: شکریہ، لیکن ابھی بہت کمزور ہے۔
lines.baca: shukriya, lekin abhī bahut kamzor hai.

lines.text: نہیں نہیں! یہ کتاب کیسی ہے؟
lines.baca: nahīñ nahīñ! ye kitāb kaisī hai?
lines.literal: no no! this book how-(f) is?

lines.text: بہت اچھی کتاب ہے، لیکن مشکل ہے۔
lines.baca: bahut achchhī kitāb hai, lekin mushkil hai.

lines.literal: very good-(f) book is, but difficult is.

lines.text: چائے بہت مزیدار ہے، اور بہت گرم بھی۔
lines.baca: chāe bahut mazedār hai, aur bahut garam bhī.
lines.id: The tea is delicious, and very hot too.
lines.literal: tea very tasty is, and very hot also.

lines.text: یہ کیفے چھوٹا ہے، لیکن بہت اچھا ہے۔
lines.baca: ye kaife chhoṭā hai, lekin bahut achchhā hai.
lines.id: This café is small, but it's very nice.
lines.literal: this café small-(m) is, but very good-(m) is.

lines.speaker: بودی:
lines.text: ہاں، اور یہاں لوگ بہت مہربان ہیں۔
lines.baca: hāñ, aur yahāñ log bahut mehrbān haiñ.
lines.id: Yes, and people here are very kind.
lines.literal: yes, and here people very kind are.

notes: **The adjective changes, not the noun.** Look at اچھی کتاب but اچھا کیفے. The word کتاب is feminine, so اچھا becomes اچھی; کیفے is masculine, so اچھا stays اچھا. The noun itself is left alone. That's the whole of this unit, and it applies in every Urdu sentence you'll ever say.

**Job titles come in pairs.** A male student is طالب علم (*tālib-e-ilm*, literally "seeker of knowledge"), a female student طالبہ (*tāliba*). The same pattern repeats in many Arabic loanwords: the ending **ـہ** marks the feminine form, just like ة in Arabic.

**Why کی and not کا in آپ کی اردو?** Because اردو is feminine. In Urdu the possessive agrees with **the thing owned**, not the owner — the opposite of most learners' instinct. Unit 4 deals with this in full; for now just notice that کی appears because of اردو, not because of آپ.

**Four adjectives that never change** appear in this dialogue: مشکل، گرم، مہربان، خالی. Notice مشکل ہے used for کتاب, which is feminine — the form stays مشکل. Adjectives that **don't end in ـا** never change, whatever the gender or number of the noun. That's big news: roughly half of all Urdu adjectives belong to this group.

**One word بہت for two jobs.** Before an adjective it means "very": بہت اچھا. Before a noun it means "many, a lot of": بہت لوگ. English uses two words; Urdu uses one. Its cousins: تھوڑا (a little), کافی (quite, enough), زیادہ (more).

**Three ways to say sorry, each with its own job.** معاف کیجیے (*ma'āf kījiye*) = "excuse me" — to interrupt, squeeze past someone, or open a question to a stranger. سنیے (*suniye*, "listen") = "excuse me" to call a waiter or vendor, and it isn't rude at all. معذرت (*ma'zerat*) is for when you're really sorry: you're late, you've spilled something.

grammars.title: Adjectives: the ones that change and the ones that don't
body: Sort every Urdu adjective into two piles and you're done with this chapter. Pile one: adjectives **ending in ـا**. These are the ones that change, and there are only three forms to learn.
Pile two: **every other adjective**. These never change, ever, under any circumstances.

head: Form
Used for
Example
Meaning
rows: a good boy · a nice house

after: The most common adjectives in pile one: بڑا (big), چھوٹا (small), نیا (new), پرانا (old), اچھا (good), برا (bad), لمبا (long, tall), موٹا (fat), ٹھنڈا (cold), سستا (cheap), مہنگا (expensive), میٹھا (sweet), کالا (black), سفید — ⚠️ سفید (white) does **not** end in ـا, so it belongs in pile two.

Pile two — never changes: مشکل (difficult), آسان (easy), گرم (hot), صاف (clean), خالی (empty), مہربان (kind), خوبصورت (beautiful), مزیدار (tasty), امیر (rich), غریب (poor), تیز (fast, spicy), دلچسپ (interesting). Notice that خالی ends in ـی yet still never changes: what counts is ـا, not ـی.

grammars.title: Guessing a noun's gender
body: No gendered language lets you guess gender a hundred percent of the time, and Urdu is no exception — کتاب is feminine while مکان is masculine for no reason anyone can explain. But a guess that's right eight times out of ten is gold in your first year, and that guess exists.
after: ⚠️ Common feminine nouns ending in a consonant that you simply have to learn: **کتاب** (book), **رات** (night), **بات** (word, matter), **چیز** (thing), **آواز** (voice, sound), **دکان** (shop), **زبان** (language, tongue), **سڑک** (road), **دیوار** (wall), **آنکھ** (eye), **ناک** (nose).

The method that actually works: **never learn a noun on its own.** Learn it with an adjective. Not "کتاب = book" but "اچھی کتاب = a good book". The gender comes along for free, and that's how every native speaker stores it.

sections.title: Jobs, qualities, and how to pay a compliment

blocks.text: Notice that most modern jobs **don't change form** — later on, only the verb will show the difference. "He/she is a doctor" is وہ ڈاکٹر ہے۔ for a man or a woman.
Twelve of the most common adjectives

blocks.title: Complimenting properly — three ready-made sentences
items: The compliment **you'll hear** most — again and again, often after you've said just three words: آپ کی اردو بہت اچھی ہے۔ ("Your Urdu is very good.") The sweetest reply: شکریہ، آپ بہت مہربان ہیں ("thank you, you're very kind").
For food: کھانا بہت مزیدار ہے۔ ("The food is delicious.") In a Pakistani home this sentence is worth more than you'd think, and it's best said before your host asks.
For a home: آپ کا گھر بہت خوبصورت ہے۔ ("Your home is beautiful.") Notice کا, not کی — what's being praised is گھر, and گھر is masculine.

blocks.title: ⚠️ Adjectives go IN FRONT of the noun
items: Good news for English speakers: Urdu puts the adjective first, just as English does — **اچھی کتاب**, *a good book*.

When the adjective is the main point of the sentence ("this book is good"), it moves to the end and ہے closes it: یہ کتاب اچھی ہے۔ The two orders mean different things: اچھی کتاب = "a good book" (a phrase), while یہ کتاب اچھی ہے = "this book is good" (a full sentence).
If you stack two adjectives, both change: بڑی نئی کتاب (a big new book).
